research.heading: What our prototype study found
research.scope: One introductory programming course. The same 60 handwritten scripts were evaluated with and without lecture context.

noContext.title: Without lecture context
noContext.result: Mean absolute error: 4.39 marks out of 60. Flagged for teacher review: 42 of 60 scripts.

withContext.title: With lecture context
withContext.result: Mean absolute error: 5.20 marks out of 60. Flagged for teacher review: 43 of 60 scripts.

research.reference: The reference averages two lecturers’ scores after applying a common scoring policy. It is a constructed reference, not independently adjudicated ground truth.
research.limits: These findings do not establish production-wide accuracy, fairness, learning gains or time savings. Most scripts were flagged for review; review effectiveness was not measured.
research.citation: Study: Teacher-in-the-Loop AI Assessment for African Classrooms (John Oghenereuse Fiewor). See the paper for methods, uncertainty and limitations.

faq.heading: Questions before you begin
faq.body: Understand the workflow, the evidence and the limits.

items.question: Can AI-generated scores replace teacher judgment?
items.answer: No. AI-generated scores and feedback can be wrong. Educators should inspect the work and review suggestions before making consequential assessment decisions.

items.question: What evidence supports GradrAI’s grading approach?
items.answer: Our 60-script research-prototype study measured scoring error and review flags in one programming course. It did not establish production-wide accuracy, fairness, time savings or learning gains. See the Research section for results and request the paper for the methods and limitations.

items.question: Which assessment formats can we discuss?
items.answer: GradrAI supports paper-based and computer-based assessment workflows. Suitability for a subject, handwriting style, diagram or answer format should be checked with representative work and the actual marking guide before a pilot.

items.question: Can we use our own marking guide?
items.answer: Yes. Provide your criteria, point allocations and acceptable approaches. Make partial-credit and follow-through rules explicit, then review whether the scoring suggestions apply them as intended.

items.question: How long does grading take?
items.answer: Turnaround depends on script volume, legibility, assessment complexity, processing mode and staff review. A pilot should establish a realistic timeframe for your assessment; we do not promise one turnaround for every workload.

items.question: Can a learner ask for human review?
items.answer: Learners should contact their course instructor about a score or explanation they believe is incorrect. Institutions should define their human-review and appeal arrangements before using AI-assisted marks.

items.question: What should we know about student data?
items.answer: Assessment workflows can involve external service providers. Read our Privacy Policy and discuss your institution’s processing, access, retention and deletion requirements with us before uploading student material. Do not send student records through the inquiry form.

items.question: Does GradrAI work offline?
items.answer: Offline support depends on the workflow and setup. Ask us about desktop and local-network assessment options for low-connectivity settings. Do not assume every AI feature works without an internet connection.

items.question: What should we know about exam-monitoring controls?
items.answer: Some strict browser-based exam workflows use fullscreen and focus checks and may submit an attempt when focus or fullscreen is lost. These signals are not proof of cheating. Agree settings and accommodations with staff before an exam.

items.question: What should an institutional pilot cover?
items.answer: Start with a defined course and assessment. Agree the materials, review responsibilities, student communication, data requirements, contingency arrangements and measures of success before using the workflow for consequential decisions.
